text: Dehydration: In physiology, dehydration is a lack of total body water that disrupts metabolic processes. It occurs when free water loss exceeds intake, often resulting from excessive sweating, health conditions, or inadequate consumption of water.
Fatigue: Fatigue is a state of being without energy for a prolonged period of time. The word fatigue is used in two contexts: in the medical sense, and in the sense of normal tiredness.

Fever: Fever or pyrexia in humans is a symptom of an anti-infection defense mechanism that appears with body temperature exceeding the normal range caused by an increase in the body's temperature set point in the hypothalamus. There is no single agreed-upon upper limit for normal temperature: sources use values ranging between 37.2 and 38.3 °C in humans.
Generalized weakness: A presenting complaint characterised by generalized weakness.

Loss of appetite: Anorexia is a medical term for loss of appetite. While the term outside of the scientific literature is often used interchangeably with anorexia nervosa, many possible causes exist for a loss of appetite, some of which may be harmless, while others indicate a serious clinical condition or pose a significant risk.
Night sweats: Night sweats or nocturnal hyperhydrosis is the repeated occurrence of excessive sweating during sleep. The person may or may not also perspire excessively while awake.

Weight loss: In medicine, health, or physical fitness, weight loss is a reduction of the total body mass, by a mean loss of fluid, body fat, or lean mass. Weight loss can either occur unintentionally because of malnourishment or an underlying disease, or from a conscious effort to improve an actual or perceived overweight or obese state.

Associated symptoms: Fear Of Gaining Weight, Strong Desire To Be Thin, Food Restrictions. Risk factors: Unknown. Age relevance: . Sex relevance: . Acute or chronic: .

Anorexia nervosa, binge eating/purging type, mild differential diagnosis notes. Compared to Anorexia Nervosa Restricting Type Mild: [LLM DRAFT] Characterized by restriction of energy intake without engaging in recurrent binge eating or purging behaviors. Compared to Anorexia Nervosa Unspecified: [LLM DRAFT] Presents with characteristic features of anorexia nervosa but lacks specific subtype documentation regarding binge-eating/purging or severity level. Compared to Myalgic Encephalomyelitischronic Fatigue Syndrome: [LLM DRAFT] Presents with profound, debilitating fatigue and post-exertional malaise rather than core psychopathology centered on body weight, distorted self-image, and intentional weight loss.

Compared to Anorexia Nervosa Restricting Type Mild: [LLM DRAFT] Higher body mass index (BMI) corresponding to the mild severity threshold rather than the extremely low BMI seen in extreme severity. Compared to Muscle Weakness Generalized: [LLM DRAFT] Presents with generalized weakness that may stem from diverse neuromuscular, metabolic, or systemic conditions rather than primary weight-related caloric deprivation and body image distortion.

Anorexia nervosa, restricting type, unspecified differential diagnosis notes. Compared to Anorexia Nervosa Binge Eatingpurging Type Mild: [LLM DRAFT] Presence of recurrent episodes of binge eating or purging behaviors such as self-induced vomiting or misuse of laxatives. Compared to Anorexia Nervosa Unspecified: [LLM DRAFT] Presentation of characteristic anorexia nervosa symptoms where specific subtyping (restricting vs. binge-eating/purging) or severity cannot be definitively determined due to insufficient clinical information.

Anorexia nervosa, unspecified differential diagnosis notes. Compared to Anorexia Nervosa Restricting Type Mild: [LLM DRAFT] Characterized by prominent caloric restriction and weight loss without binge eating or purging behaviors, with severity specified. Dehydration of newborn: A condition in which a newborn lacks adequate fluid, leading to impaired organ function. Common presenting complaints: Dehydration, Weight Loss. Associated symptoms: none listed. Risk factors: none listed. Age relevance: . Sex relevance: . Acute or chronic: .

Dehydration of newborn red flags. Red flag (RF_LETHARGY_OR_UNRESPONSIVENESS) triggered by complaint '': Newborn is unusually difficult to wake or completely unresponsive.. Red flag (RF_SEVERE_OLIGURIA_ANURIA) triggered by complaint '': No wet diapers for 6 to 8 hours or significantly decreased urine output..

Dehydration of newborn differential diagnosis notes. Compared to Hypovolemia: [LLM DRAFT] Presents with acute intravascular volume depletion due to hemorrhage or fluid shifts across all pediatric age groups, whereas neonatal dehydration is primarily characterized by hypernatremia or total body water loss often related to feeding difficulties.

Associated symptoms: Inability To Move The Facial Muscles On One Side, Change In Taste, Pain Around The Ear. Risk factors: Unknown. Age relevance: . Sex relevance: . Acute or chronic: .

Facial weakness following cerebral infarction red flags. Red flag (RF_ACUTE_STROKE_RECURRENCE) triggered by complaint '': Sudden onset of new neurological deficits such as severe headache, confusion, or sudden loss of vision.

Facial weakness following cerebral infarction differential diagnosis notes. Compared to Facial Weakness Following Nontraumatic Intracerebral Hemorrhage: [LLM DRAFT] Neuroimaging reveals acute parenchymal blood rather than an ischemic infarct. Compared to Facial Weakness Following Nontraumatic Subarachnoid Hemorrhage: [LLM DRAFT] Presence of thunderclap headache and xanthochromia or blood in the basal cisterns on imaging. Compared to Facial Weakness Following Other Cerebrovascular Disease: [LLM DRAFT] Causative etiology is a distinct vascular pathology such as cerebral venous sinus thrombosis or vascular malformation rather than thromboembolic infarction.

Facial weakness following nontraumatic intracerebral hemorrhage red flags. Red flag (RF_SUDDEN_NEUROLOGICAL_DETERIORATION) triggered by complaint '': Worsening facial weakness accompanied by acute confusion, severe headache, or altered mental status..

Facial weakness following nontraumatic intracerebral hemorrhage differential diagnosis notes. Compared to Facial Weakness Following Cerebral Infarction: [LLM DRAFT] History of ischemic rather than hemorrhagic cerebrovascular event on neuroimaging Compared to Facial Weakness Following Nontraumatic Subarachnoid Hemorrhage: [LLM DRAFT] Presence of sudden thunderclap headache and meningeal signs rather than focal intraparenchymal hematoma symptoms Compared to Facial Weakness Following Other Nontraumatic Intracranial Hemorrhage: [LLM DRAFT] Bleeding located in subdural or extradural spaces rather than primarily intracerebral tissue

Facial weakness following nontraumatic subarachnoid hemorrhage differential diagnosis notes. Compared to Facial Weakness Following Cerebral Infarction: [LLM DRAFT] History of ischemic stroke rather than subarachnoid hemorrhage on neuroimaging. Compared to Facial Weakness Following Nontraumatic Intracerebral Hemorrhage: [LLM DRAFT] Primary parenchymal hemorrhage on neuroimaging rather than subarachnoid blood. Compared to Facial Weakness Following Other Nontraumatic Intracranial Hemorrhage: [LLM DRAFT] Intracranial hemorrhage originating from an alternate non-subarachnoid source.

Facial weakness following other cerebrovascular disease red flags. Red flag (RF_ACUTE_STROKE_SYMPTOMS) triggered by complaint '': Sudden onset of new neurological deficits, severe headache, confusion, or sudden severe weakness on one side of the body..

Facial weakness following other cerebrovascular disease differential diagnosis notes. Compared to Facial Weakness Following Nontraumatic Subarachnoid Hemorrhage: [LLM DRAFT] Often accompanied by a sudden, severe 'thunderclap' headache and meningeal signs rather than isolated focal deficits.

Facial weakness following other nontraumatic intracranial hemorrhage differential diagnosis notes. Compared to Facial Weakness Following Nontraumatic Intracerebral Hemorrhage: [LLM DRAFT] Associated primarily with a parenchymal bleed rather than other nontraumatic intracranial hemorrhage locations (such as subdural or epidural). Compared to Facial Weakness Following Nontraumatic Subarachnoid Hemorrhage: [LLM DRAFT] Typically preceded by a sudden 'thunderclap' headache rather than other forms of nontraumatic intracranial hemorrhage. Compared to Facial Weakness Following Cerebral Infarction: [LLM DRAFT] Caused by ischemic tissue infarction rather than a primary intracranial hemorrhage.

Facial weakness following unspecified cerebrovascular disease differential diagnosis notes. Compared to Facial Weakness Following Cerebral Infarction: [LLM DRAFT] Confirmed by neuroimaging demonstrating ischemic infarct rather than unspecified vascular etiology. Compared to Facial Weakness Following Nontraumatic Intracerebral Hemorrhage: [LLM DRAFT] Confirmed by neuroimaging showing acute primary parenchymal bleeding. Compared to Facial Weakness Following Nontraumatic Subarachnoid Hemorrhage: [LLM DRAFT] Typically accompanied by sudden 'thunderclap' headache and meningeal signs rather than isolated vascular deficit.

Heat fatigue, transient, initial encounter: A brief episode of fatigue and malaise precipitated by excessive heat exposure, resolving with rest and hydration. Common presenting complaints: Fatigue. Associated symptoms: none listed. Risk factors: none listed. Age relevance: . Sex relevance: . Acute or chronic: .

Heat fatigue, transient, initial encounter red flags. Red flag (RF_ALTERED_MENTAL_STATUS) triggered by complaint '': Confusion, lethargy, disorientation, or loss of consciousness suggesting progression to heat stroke.. Red flag (RF_HIGH_CORE_BODY_TEMPERATURE) triggered by complaint '': Core body temperature exceeding 104°F (40°C) indicating severe heat illness..

Heat fatigue, transient, initial encounter differential diagnosis notes. Compared to Heat Fatigue Transient Subsequent Encounter: [LLM DRAFT] Represents a follow-up visit for previously diagnosed heat fatigue rather than a new initial presentation. Compared to Hypovolemia: [LLM DRAFT] Characterized by significant intravascular volume depletion and hemodynamic instability independent of ambient temperature exposure. Compared to Dehydration Of Newborn: [LLM DRAFT] Presents specifically in neonates with inadequate fluid intake or excessive loss, unrelated to environmental heat stress.

Heat fatigue, transient, sequela: Persistent fatigue and malaise following an episode of heat fatigue, typically resolving within days but may linger as a transient sequela. Common presenting complaints: Fatigue. Associated symptoms: none listed. Risk factors: none listed. Age relevance: . Sex relevance: . Acute or chronic: .

Heat fatigue, transient, sequela red flags. Red flag (RF_ALTERED_MENTAL_STATUS) triggered by complaint '': Confusion, lethargy, or loss of consciousness following heat exposure. Red flag (RF_HIGH_BODY_TEMPERATURE) triggered by complaint '': Core body temperature exceeding 104°F (40°C).

Heat fatigue, transient, sequela differential diagnosis notes. Compared to Heat Fatigue Transient Initial Encounter: [LLM DRAFT] Presents during or immediately after acute heat exposure rather than as a delayed or chronic sequela. Compared to Myalgic Encephalomyelitischronic Fatigue Syndrome: [LLM DRAFT] Characterized by long-term, relapsing fatigue and post-exertional malaise independent of a history of heat exposure. Compared to Hypovolemia: [LLM DRAFT] Manifests primarily with signs of acute intravascular volume depletion such as hypotension and tachycardia, which may occur without environmental heat exposure.

Heat fatigue, transient, subsequent encounter: A temporary state of exhaustion and reduced physical performance following exposure to high temperatures. Common presenting complaints: Fatigue. Associated symptoms: none listed. Risk factors: none listed. Age relevance: . Sex relevance: . Acute or chronic: .

Heat fatigue, transient, subsequent encounter red flags. Red flag (RF_HEAT_STROKE) triggered by complaint '': Altered mental status, confusion, loss of consciousness, or a body temperature above 104°F (40°C). Red flag (RF_SEVERE_DEHYDRATION) triggered by complaint '': Inability to retain fluids, extreme dizziness, or absence of urination.

Heat fatigue, transient, subsequent encounter differential diagnosis notes. Compared to Heat Fatigue Transient Initial Encounter: [LLM DRAFT] Presents during the acute exposure episode rather than as a follow-up visit for a resolved or ongoing prior event. Compared to Heat Fatigue Transient Sequela: [LLM DRAFT] Represents a chronic, long-term residual complication rather than a routine subsequent clinical encounter for recent heat fatigue. Compared to Hypovolemia: [LLM DRAFT] Characterized by objective signs of significant intravascular volume depletion and electrolyte imbalance rather than isolated heat-induced fatigue symptoms.

Hypovolemia: Hypovolemia, also known as volume depletion or volume contraction, is a state of abnormally low extracellular fluid in the body. This may be due to either a loss of both salt and water or a decrease in blood volume. Common presenting complaints: Dehydration. Associated symptoms: Headache, Fatigue, Nausea, Profuse Sweating, Dizziness. Risk factors: none listed. Age relevance: . Sex relevance: . Acute or chronic: .

Hypovolemia red flags. Red flag (RF_SEVERE_HYPOTENSION_OR_SHOCK) triggered by complaint '': Blood pressure drops significantly with symptoms of confusion, dizziness, or cold, clammy skin.. Red flag (RF_ANURIA) triggered by complaint '': Complete lack of urination for 8 hours or more, indicating acute kidney injury..

Hypovolemia differential diagnosis notes. Compared to Dehydration Of Newborn: [LLM DRAFT] Presents with sunken fontanelles, lethargy, and inadequate wet diapers specific to neonatal physiology and feeding issues. Compared to Anorexia Nervosa Restricting Type Mild: [LLM DRAFT] Characterized by self-imposed severe caloric restriction and distorted body image rather than acute fluid or blood loss. Compared to Heat Fatigue Transient Initial Encounter: [LLM DRAFT] Presents with temporary heat-related discomfort and fatigue without the profound intravascular volume depletion or hemodynamic instability seen in hypovolemia.

Lassa fever: Lassa fever, also known as Lassa hemorrhagic fever, is a type of viral hemorrhagic fever caused by the Lassa virus. Many of those infected by the virus do not develop symptoms. Common presenting complaints: Fever, Night Sweats. Associated symptoms: Fever, Headaches, Bleeding. Risk factors: Lassa Virus. Age relevance: . Sex relevance: . Acute or chronic: .

Lassa fever red flags. Red flag (RF_HEMORRHAGIC_MANIFESTATIONS) triggered by complaint '': Bleeding from gums, eyes, nose, or gastrointestinal tract in a suspected patient.. Red flag (RF_NEUROLOGICAL_DETERIORATION) triggered by complaint '': Onset of confusion, seizures, or coma..

Lassa fever differential diagnosis notes. Compared to Paratyphoid Fever A: [LLM DRAFT] Accompanied by gastrointestinal symptoms like constipation or diarrhea with relative bradycardia rather than prominent hemorrhagic manifestations. Compared to Typhoid Fever Unspecified: [LLM DRAFT] Characterized by a step-ladder fever pattern, rose spots on the trunk, and hepatosplenomegaly without the mucosal bleeding typical of Lassa fever. Compared to Q Fever: [LLM DRAFT] Presents predominantly with atypical pneumonia and a history of livestock exposure rather than acute viral hemorrhagic fever features.

Muscle weakness (generalized): Muscle weakness is a lack of muscle strength. Its causes are numerous and can be divided into conditions associated with either true or perceived muscle weakness. Common presenting complaints: Generalized Weakness. Associated symptoms: none listed. Risk factors: none listed. Age relevance: . Sex relevance: . Acute or chronic: .

Muscle weakness (generalized) red flags. Red flag (RF_ACUTE_RESPIRATORY_COMPROMISE) triggered by complaint '': Generalized muscle weakness accompanied by shortness of breath, difficulty swallowing, or inability to lift the head.. Red flag (RF_SUDDEN_ONSET_FOCAL_NEUROLOGICAL_DEFICITS) triggered by complaint '': Generalized weakness accompanied by sudden facial droop, slurred speech, or loss of vision..

Muscle weakness (generalized) differential diagnosis notes. Compared to Myalgic Encephalomyelitischronic Fatigue Syndrome: [LLM DRAFT] Characterized by post-exertional malaise and profound fatigue rather than true objective neuromuscular weakness. Compared to Postviral Fatigue Syndrome: [LLM DRAFT] Presents with persistent generalized exhaustion and lethargy following a documented viral infection, lacking primary muscle pathology. Compared to Hypovolemia: [LLM DRAFT] Manifests with acute circulatory compromise, tachycardia, and orthostatic hypotension rather than primary neuromuscular weakness.

Myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome: Myalgic encephalomyelitis​/​chronic fatigue syndrome (ME/CFS) is a disabling chronic illness. People with ME/CFS experience profound fatigue that does not go away with rest, as well as problems with sleep and memory or concentration. Common presenting complaints: Fatigue. Associated symptoms: Worsening Of Symptoms With Activity, Long Term Fatigue, Sleep Problems, Others. Risk factors: Unknown. Age relevance: . Sex relevance: . Acute or chronic: .

Myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome red flags. Red flag (RF_SEVERE_PROGRESSIVE_NEUROLOGICAL_DEFICITS) triggered by complaint '': Rapid onset of focal deficits, severe cognitive decline, or new-onset seizures not explained by ME/CFS.. Red flag (RF_SUICIDAL_IDEATION) triggered by complaint '': Expression of hopelessness, self-harm thoughts, or suicidal intent due to chronic suffering..

Myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome differential diagnosis notes. Compared to Other Post Infection And Related Fatigue Syndromes: [LLM DRAFT] A clear temporal link to a documented non-viral infection rather than the multi-system criteria required for ME/CFS. Compared to Postviral Fatigue Syndrome: [LLM DRAFT] Presents as prolonged fatigue specifically following a recognized viral illness without the full constellation of ME/CFS neuroimmune and autonomic symptoms. Compared to Muscle Weakness Generalized: [LLM DRAFT] Characterized by a primary decrease in maximal voluntary muscle force rather than the hallmark post-exertional malaise (PEM) seen in ME/CFS.

Other post infection and related fatigue syndromes: A persistent fatigue syndrome that arises after an acute infection, characterized by profound tiredness lasting more than 6 weeks, often accompanied by cognitive dysfunction and post-exertional malaise. Common presenting complaints: Fatigue. Associated symptoms: Chronic Fatigue. Risk factors: Unknown. Age relevance: . Sex relevance: . Acute or chronic: .

Other post infection and related fatigue syndromes red flags. Red flag (RF_SEVERE_NEUROLOGICAL_DEFICITS) triggered by complaint '': Acute onset of focal weakness, confusion, seizures, or severe altered mental status. Red flag (RF_PROGRESSIVE_CARDIOPULMONARY_SYMPTOMS) triggered by complaint '': New or worsening chest pain, severe dyspnea at rest, or syncope.

Other post infection and related fatigue syndromes differential diagnosis notes. Compared to Myalgic Encephalomyelitischronic Fatigue Syndrome: [LLM DRAFT] Characterized by post-exertional malaise, unrefreshing sleep, and cognitive impairment lasting at least six months without a confirmed preceding acute infection. Compared to Postviral Fatigue Syndrome: [LLM DRAFT] Follows a definitively identified viral infection rather than other types of pathogens or unspecified infectious agents. Compared to Heat Fatigue Transient Initial Encounter: [LLM DRAFT] Presents with acute fatigue and exhaustion directly linked to environmental heat exposure rather than an antecedent infection.

Paratyphoid fever A: A systemic infection caused by Salmonella Paratyphi A, presenting with prolonged fever, abdominal pain, and gastrointestinal symptoms. Sandfly fever differential diagnosis notes. Compared to Lassa Fever: [LLM DRAFT] Presents with prominent mucosal bleeding, pharyngitis with exudates, and sensorineural hearing loss, unlike the typically self-limiting febrile nature of sandfly fever. Common presenting complaints: Fever, Night Sweats. Associated symptoms: Fever. Risk factors: Infected Insect Bite. Age relevance: . Sex relevance: . Acute or chronic: .
